setup: Mao Zedong dies on September 9, 1976, and a month later his chosen successor arrests Mao's widow and her three allies, the Gang of Four who ran the Cultural Revolution. That ends the Maoist era by force, but it answers nothing. China has nearly a billion people, is poorer per person than most of sub-Saharan Africa, has had its universities shut for a decade, runs on ration coupons, and has spent twenty-seven years convulsed by its own government. The only legitimating idea anyone in power holds is the thought of the man who caused the worst famine in history. Who governs, and on what basis, is wide open. For two years it looks like the answer will be more of the same, only quieter, under the colorless Hua Guofeng, whose entire claim to rule is that Mao picked him. The deeper question this whole book turns on is being set right here: in post-Mao China, can legitimacy ever again come from anything but results?

bridge: Chapter 1 left Mao dead, Hua Guofeng sidelined, and Deng Xiaoping installed as paramount leader on a single radical idea: that policy should be judged by whether it works, not whether it matches Mao's words. The December 1978 Third Plenum made it official, shifting the party's central task from class struggle to economic construction and opening the reform era. But that is the story from the top, in Beijing, among men in meetings. The first and largest escape from poverty did not start there at all. It started in a starving village, as a crime.
setup: The reform era is usually told as Deng, the cities, and foreign money — and those come later. The first move happens in the countryside, fast, from below. Mao's people's communes farmed land collectively: the harvest went to the state, individual effort earned near-meaningless work points, and one of Earth's most fertile farming civilizations could not feed itself. In December 1978, eighteen starving households in Xiaogang, Anhui secretly carve up their collective land, agree each family will meet the state quota and keep the rest, and fingerprint a contract pledging to raise one another's children if any of them is executed for it. The next harvest explodes — not from new tools or seed, but because effort is finally tied to reward. The question hanging over the chapter is whether Beijing will punish this as the capital offense it technically is, or claim it. The men who decide will run the reform machine and, two of them, be destroyed by it.

bridge: Chapter 2 showed the rural half of Deng's reform: break the communes, let families keep the surplus, and watch incomes double within six years, with no foreign money in it at all. Surplus farm labor, blocked from the cities by the hukou registration system, poured into small rural factories that outgrew state industry. That demonstration — that production for the market beats production for the plan — ran entirely on Chinese soil. Now comes the half the world actually watched: opening a country that had spent thirty years in near-total isolation to global capitalism.
setup: Deng's instrument is geographic and deliberately small: fenced-off zones where the rules of the planned economy are suspended and foreign capitalism is allowed to operate, so that if it fails or contaminates the system the damage stays contained. In 1979–80 four Special Economic Zones go up on the southern coast, the most famous being Shenzhen, a stretch of paddies and fishing villages across the border from Hong Kong. The site is chosen not for resources but for adjacency to capital — Hong Kong's money, factory know-how, and Cantonese-speaking entrepreneurs with mainland family. For the first decade the investment is overwhelmingly overseas Chinese capital, not Western multinationals, moving factories a few miles into a workforce that costs a tenth as much. Shenzhen becomes a city of millions in a generation. But none of it is ideologically comfortable, and the live question of elite politics for fifteen years is blunt: is this socialist, or is it capitalist?

bridge: The reform so far has been comparatively easy. Chapter 2's rural break and Chapter 3's coastal zones both worked by stepping aside and letting market incentives loose at the margins, and the results — doubled farm incomes, a boomtown rising at a floor every few days — were spectacular. But that was the simple half. The state still owned the heavy industry, set the prices, and lived in the cities, where a sudden jump in the cost of food and fuel could mean unrest. Reforming that — the urban, industrial core — is the hard problem, and the way it half-works and half-fails is the machinery of the explosion to come.
setup: In 1984 the party extends reform to the cities and state factories with a hybrid device, the dual-track price system: the same commodity — steel, coal, cement — carries two prices at once, a low planned price for the quota and a high market price for anything above it. The theory is elegant; the side effect is corrosive. Anyone who can buy at the planned price and sell at the market price doubles their money for nothing, and the people positioned to do exactly that are officials and their children, who control the quotas. This is guandao, official profiteering, and it puts the word princelings into Chinese politics for good. Meanwhile a 1988 attempt to free prices in one push triggers double-digit inflation and panic bank runs, the reformers retreat discredited, and the leadership splits openly. Over all of it sits a decade of restless intellectual ferment. By the spring of 1989 the country is a fast, unequal, inflationary boom that has enriched the connected and frightened everyone else — and the students who grew up arguing about whether tradition itself is the problem are primed and waiting for an occasion to gather.

bridge: Chapter 4 left China in a dangerous state: a fast, unequal boom that had enriched the connected through guandao profiteering, double-digit inflation eating ordinary wages, a stalled and discredited reform, and a leadership split openly between Zhao Ziyang's accelerators and the conservatives. A decade of intellectual ferment had primed a student generation to argue that something was deeply wrong. All they lacked was an occasion to gather in the open — and in April 1989 a funeral provided one. This is the hinge of the entire book.
setup: This is the moment the 1979 bargain — prosperity for a monopoly on power — is challenged head-on and defended with the army, and it is also one of the most contested events in modern history, contested down to the basic facts. It begins with a death: Hu Yaobang, the liberal party chief purged in 1987, dies in April 1989, and mourning a disgraced reformer becomes the only legal way to make a political statement. Students pour into Tiananmen Square; the mourning becomes a sit-in, the sit-in a movement demanding action on corruption, inflation, and press freedom, not mostly Western democracy in the abstract. It draws in workers, which is what makes it lethal to a leadership that knows worker-student alliances have brought down dynasties. A hunger strike timed to a Soviet summit humiliates the government before the world's press, the leadership splits over force, and Deng sides with force. The chapter applies this series' contested-claims rule at its hardest: the most basic number, how many were killed, is genuinely not known, and is given as a range.

bridge: Chapter 5 ended with the army clearing central Beijing by force in June 1989, the reformers Hu and Zhao gone, and China an international pariah. The party had drawn its lesson: political liberalization is an existential threat. The conservatives, apparently vindicated, were ascendant and moving to roll the whole reform project back. Then, across 1989–91, the entire Communist world outside China collapsed — the Berlin Wall, Eastern Europe, and at the end of 1991 the Soviet Union itself, the model on which the whole system was built, simply ceased to exist. In 1990 it looked as though China might freeze into a poorer, harder, more isolated version of itself.
setup: It does the opposite, and the turn is the most counterintuitive in the story. The hardliners read the Soviet collapse as a command to tighten everything. Deng reads it the other way, in the book's key strategic judgment: the USSR died because it reformed politics without delivering economic goods, so the only thing that can save the Chinese Communist Party is to grow the economy so fast and so undeniably that prosperity, not ideology, becomes the basis of consent. In early 1992, eighty-seven years old and holding no office, Deng takes a train south to the boom zones and, in remarks the central propaganda apparatus tries to bury, demands that reform accelerate and that whoever opposes it step down. The provincial officials getting rich mobilize behind him, the conservative line is routed, and the Party Congress adopts the goal of a socialist market economy — finally, officially ending the thirty-year question of whether markets are allowed. The floodgates open under a new leadership Deng has installed, and the deepest test of his life's work is still to come: whether the system he built can survive his own death.

bridge: Chapter 6 turned the post-Tiananmen freeze into the greatest boom in history. Deng's 1992 Southern Tour routed the conservatives, the party adopted the socialist market economy, and a new leadership — Jiang Zemin and the technocrat premier Zhu Rongji — executed a takeoff funded by a 1994 tax reform that recentralized money in Beijing. Deng died in 1997, and his deepest achievement proved itself: the machine kept running with no succession war. Now China stops being a large country that exports cheap goods and becomes structurally fused to the global economy.
setup: Three things happen close together between 1997 and 2002, and the leadership handles all three from the same conviction — that economic results are the only thing standing between the party and the Soviet fate. On July 1, 1997, Hong Kong reverts to Chinese sovereignty after 155 years of British rule under the formula "one country, two systems," which promises the city its capitalism, courts, and free press until 2047 — and whose underlying bet, that those freedoms can be quarantined behind a system boundary like the Special Economic Zones, the book will test in Chapter 13. Almost immediately the Asian Financial Crisis wrecks the region's miracle economies while a more-closed China stands firm, drawing a lasting lesson about the dangers of open capital. At home, Zhu Rongji forces through the brutal restructuring of the state factories, laying off tens of millions and ending Maoist urban socialism by the party's own hand. And the capstone, in 2001, is accession to the World Trade Organization — championed in the West on an explicit theory the chapter has to weigh against what actually happened.

bridge: Chapter 7 fused China to the world economy: Hong Kong returned, China weathered the Asian crisis by holding its currency steady, Zhu Rongji laid off tens of millions of state workers, and 2001 WTO accession locked in market access and quadrupled exports. The Western bet behind it all was that trade would liberalize China politically — and the 1999 crushing of Falun Gong already hinted that the bet would lose. Now the export machine runs at full throttle under a new leadership, and the country becomes, in fact and not just slogan, the factory of the world.
setup: The decade from 2002 to 2012, under Hu Jintao and premier Wen Jiabao, is the boom in its purest form. The engine has a human name: roughly 200 to 300 million migrant workers who leave the countryside for the coastal factory cities and who, because of the Mao-era hukou registration system, are legally non-residents where they work — unable to enroll their children in local schools or claim local benefits, cheap and mobile and disenfranchised by design. On their backs China lifts, by the World Bank's much-repeated figure, roughly 800 million people out of extreme poverty, the largest and fastest such reduction in history, and builds the physical infrastructure of a developed economy within a single working life. But the same decade brings the costs due: inequality among the world's highest, a wrecked environment, metastasizing corruption, and a scandal genre — poisoned baby formula, collapsing buildings, the concealed SARS epidemic of 2003 — all tracing to one root, an economy moving faster than any accountability the political system will permit. Both the triumph and the rot are true, and they are the same story.

bridge: Chapter 8 was the boom at full throttle: under Hu Jintao and Wen Jiabao, migrant labor built the factory of the world, some 800 million people climbed out of poverty, and the costs — inequality, environmental ruin, the scandal genre running from poisoned formula to the SARS cover-up — all traced to an economy outrunning any accountability the system allowed. The model had reached its peak and accumulated its contradictions. Then a single year compressed the triumph, the tragedy, the scandal, and the decision that would mortgage everything after into twelve months.
setup: 2008 is the inflection point of the entire story. The triumph is the Beijing Summer Olympics, whose opening ceremony in the Bird's Nest stadium is staged explicitly to announce that the century of humiliation is over and China has resumed its place as a first-rank civilization — the emotional payoff of thirty years of the bargain. The tragedy comes three months earlier: a magnitude-7.9 earthquake kills nearly 70,000 in Sichuan, a disproportionate number of them schoolchildren crushed in shoddy "tofu-dreg" schools while sturdier buildings stood, exposing the corruption the era's slogans had named but not fixed. Then, in September, the Western financial system collapses, Chinese exports fall off a cliff, tens of thousands of factories close, and twenty million-plus migrants lose their jobs — and for the first time since 1989 the prosperity half of the bargain looks genuinely at risk. The leadership's answer is a four-trillion-yuan stimulus, one of the largest in history relative to the economy, that works spectacularly in the short run and builds the trap the final chapters describe.

bridge: Chapter 9 made 2008 the hinge: the Olympics announced China's arrival, the Sichuan earthquake exposed the corruption beneath the boom, the Western crash threatened the export engine, and a four-trillion-yuan stimulus saved growth while quietly building a debt-and-construction trap. The stimulus papered over the model's costs without fixing them. Now those costs become undeniable, a brief opening lets the public say so, and a once-a-decade leadership handover turns into the most dangerous elite crisis since Tiananmen — and produces the man who would define the next decade.
setup: The years 2009 to 2012 are the system's hangover. The stimulus has inflated property beyond what ordinary workers can afford, left ghost cities and a mountain of local-government debt, and widened the gap between the connected rich and everyone else into the society's defining feature. For a few years there is an unprecedented place to say so: Weibo, launched in 2009, creates the first fast, national, semi-public square in PRC history, where scandals like the 2011 Wenzhou high-speed-rail crash and its attempted cover-up go viral before the censors catch up. The regime's nerves show — a wildly disproportionate crackdown on phantom "Jasmine" gatherings, the Nobel given to the jailed dissident Liu Xiaobo. Into this comes the succession crisis: Bo Xilai, a charismatic princeling running Chongqing on Mao-nostalgic populism, is openly campaigning for the apex in a system where campaigning is forbidden — until the affair detonates and the frightened elite reaches for a safe, dull compromise candidate.

bridge: Chapter 10 was the disaffected decade and the knife fight at the top. The post-2008 stimulus had papered over the model's costs with debt; Weibo briefly let the public see and say what was wrong; and the Bo Xilai affair turned the 2012 succession into the gravest elite rupture since Tiananmen. Out of the wreckage the frightened elite elevated a man it believed was a dull, reliable consensus technocrat in the Jiang–Hu mold, who would preside over collective leadership, term limits, and the quiet enrichment of the families at the top. They could not have been more wrong.
setup: Within five years Xi Jinping has concentrated more personal power than anyone since Mao, reversed the central political achievement of the Deng era, and turned the party from a machine for managing growth into an instrument of one man's will. His instrument is an anti-corruption campaign whose genius is that the corruption is completely real — over a million officials disciplined, including the former security overlord Zhou Yongkang, the most senior figure ever prosecuted in the PRC. It is at once a genuine attack on a corruption that was strangling the country and the most effective purge of rivals in modern Chinese politics, and the two are inseparable. The ideological turn matches it: the "Chinese Dream" of national rejuvenation, Document No. 9 ordering the apparatus to combat constitutional democracy and a free press, the closing of the Weibo opening, the gutting of the human-rights bar. The capstone, in 2018, is the abolition of the presidential two-term limit — reopening, deliberately, the two-thousand-year problem Deng had solved.

bridge: Chapter 11 was the consolidation of power at home: within five years Xi Jinping had used a genuine anti-corruption campaign to purge his rivals, fused party rule to the "Chinese Dream" of national rejuvenation, closed the Weibo opening with Document No. 9, and in 2018 abolished the presidential term limit, reopening the succession problem Deng had solved. With control secured inside the system, the same drive now turns outward — and downward, onto China's own citizens.
setup: This chapter is the projection of Xi's power in two directions that are really one project. The outward project is the Belt and Road Initiative, announced in 2013: a vast program of Chinese-financed and Chinese-built infrastructure across Asia, Africa, Latin America, and into Europe — the largest development-finance push since the Marshall Plan, an outlet for the steel and cement the post-2008 economy can no longer absorb at home, and a statement that the world economic order will now have a Chinese pole. The downward project is the most comprehensive domestic-surveillance apparatus in history. The book applies its contested-claims rule hard here: the "debt-trap diplomacy" charge is mostly overstated by careful research, and the unified national "social credit score" of Western imagination never actually existed — but the real blacklists, the pervasive cameras, and above all what was done in Xinjiang are grim enough without exaggeration. There, from around 2017, the state turned the apparatus fully on the Uyghurs, and the numbers and even the word for it are contested down to the ground.

bridge: Chapter 12 projected Xi's power outward through the Belt and Road and downward through the surveillance state, culminating in the mass internment of the Uyghurs in Xinjiang — the apparatus turned fully on. That was control imposed where Beijing held undisputed sovereignty. This chapter is about the two places where its sovereignty was either qualified by promise or rejected outright, and where the book's central contradiction — a regime that delivers prosperity but cannot tolerate autonomous political life — became impossible to paper over.
setup: Recall the bet from Chapter 7: when Hong Kong returned in 1997, "one country, two systems" promised its capitalist economy, independent courts, and free press until 2047, on the theory that those freedoms could be quarantined behind a system boundary the way the Special Economic Zones quarantined capitalism. For about fifteen years the quarantine mostly held. Then it failed in stages — the 2014 Umbrella Movement, the abduction of five booksellers, and finally the 2019 extradition-bill protests that put a quarter to a third of the whole population into the streets, the gravest challenge to Beijing since 1989. Beijing's 2020 National Security Law ended the protests, the opposition, and the free press at once. And across the strait sits Taiwan, governed since 1949 by the side that lost the Chinese civil war, now a genuine democracy that has watched Hong Kong's "two systems" be dismantled and drawn the opposite lesson. This is the one major thread the entire series cannot close, because it is not closed.

bridge: Chapter 13 showed the book's contradiction breaking into the open in Hong Kong and Taiwan: the 2020 National Security Law gutted Hong Kong's freedoms, and watching it dismantled pushed a democratic Taiwan further away, leaving the most dangerous flashpoint on Earth unresolved. For thirty years the larger frame around all of this had been engagement — the Western and especially American assumption that integrating China would make it richer, more like its partners, and a stakeholder in the existing order. This chapter is the period when both sides finally admitted that assumption had failed.
setup: Roughly between 2017 and 2022 the relationship flips from engagement to open strategic rivalry, the defining geopolitical fact of the present. The economic break comes as a trade war: from 2018 the United States imposes tariffs on hundreds of billions of dollars of Chinese goods, citing the deficit, forced technology transfer, and the explicit threat of the Made in China 2025 plan. The deeper and more lasting conflict is a chip war — the US and its allies cutting China off from the most advanced semiconductors and the equipment to make them, the single most serious external constraint on the Chinese model. The arrest of Huawei's Meng Wanzhou and China's hostage-style detention of two Canadians make it concrete; engagement gives way to "decoupling." China's diplomacy hardens to match, into combative "wolf-warrior" nationalism that plays well at home and badly everywhere else, accelerating the very encirclement it reacts to. Two confrontations — the rejected South China Sea ruling and the deadly Galwan Valley clash with India — show the new logic and revive this series' longest-running comparison.

bridge: Across fourteen chapters the bargain held: from Deng's first reforms through WTO accession, the factory-of-the-world boom, and the 2008 stimulus, the party delivered prosperity, and in exchange kept its absolute monopoly on power. Under Xi that monopoly hardened — the term limit gone, the surveillance state built, Hong Kong crushed, and engagement with the West collapsed into open rivalry. But every chapter has also tracked a single recurring flaw: a system that can mobilize like no other and cannot correct itself, because correction means telling the leader he is wrong. This final chapter is where that flaw, and the prosperity that masked it, are both put to the test at once.
setup: The book ends where the present begins, and it is too recent for verdicts. A virus emerges in Wuhan in late 2019; in a rerun of the SARS cover-up, officials silence the doctor Li Wenliang, who is forced to recant, catches it, and dies — a grief the censors briefly cannot contain. Then the state pivots to what it does best: an unprecedented 76-day lockdown and a national zero-COVID apparatus that, for roughly two years, genuinely works and is broadcast as proof the system is superior to the death-tolerant democracies. Then it inverts. The two-month confinement of twenty-five million people in Shanghai breaks the public's patience and the economy's momentum, the November 2022 white-paper protests become the broadest open defiance since 1989, and zero-COVID is abandoned overnight with no preparation. Meanwhile the prosperity half of the bargain falters for the first time in forty years — the property sector cracks, youth unemployment hits unpublished records, and the population begins to shrink. The series that has always known how its stories ended must stop here and admit that no one knows how this one does.
